learn.prompt: An 80 N stone rests 1 m left of the fulcrum. Move the 20 N effort until the lever balances.
learn.hint: The lever multiplies your 20 N effort into 80 N when the effort arm is 80 / 20 = 4 times longer.
learn.explanation: With an effort arm of 4 m and a load arm of 1 m, the Ideal Mechanical Advantage is 4 / 1 = 4. The 20 N effort balances an 80 N load.

learn.prompt: A crowbar provides an Ideal Mechanical Advantage (IMA) of 5. How much effort is needed to lift a 250 N crate?
learn.explanation: Dividing the 250 N load by the IMA of 5 gives an effort of 50 N.

misconceptionMap.b: An IMA of 5 multiplies your force, so you need much less than the full 250 N.
misconceptionMap.c: That multiplies the load by 5 instead of dividing it.
misconceptionMap.d: That would only be an IMA of 2.5.

check.prompt: A 60 N load sits 1 m left of the pivot. Where must a 15 N effort be applied to balance it?
check.hint: Match the torques: 60 N x 1 m = 15 N x d.
check.explanation: 60 N m / 15 N = 4 m. The machine provides an IMA of 4.

check.prompt: A machine multiplies force by 4 (IMA = 4). To lift a load upward by 0.5 m, how far must you push the effort handle?
check.hint: Work in equals work out: effort distance = load height x IMA.
check.explanation: Because force is multiplied by 4, you must move 4 times farther: 0.5 m x 4 = 2.0 m.

misconceptionMap.a: That divides distance by 4; you must push farther to make up for using less force.
misconceptionMap.b: That would mean no trade-off between force and distance.
misconceptionMap.d: That multiplies by 8 instead of the IMA of 4.

takeaway.title: Machines multiply force, not energy
takeaway.body: Mechanical advantage tells you how many times a machine multiplies your input force. Because work is conserved, any gain in force requires a proportional increase in the distance the effort moves.
